It is the common tool of all the people belonging to a particular society or people, both in matters they share and in matters on which they differ.
The reason is that language does not itself reflect the social relations in which class and group conflicts are contained.

Instead, it directly reflects people’s everyday activity in the broad areas of life they share—areas in which individuals from every class and every social group meet and communicate with one another through the same language.
This is also the source of the historical character of language.
It comes from this direct and simple relationship across the shared life of society, a relationship that continues throughout the society’s history even as one social structure gives way to another.
Language therefore carries the unity of that history through the continuing unity of the language itself, despite all the breaks, contradictions, and conflicts contained within the history.
For the same reason, when studying language in a subject such as ours, we must see it as organically connected with the history of the society to which it belongs.
And this same connection necessarily links language to the culture of that society.
Its culture is, first, a product of its history.
Its language is, second, the means through which that cultural product is expressed.

Given this view of language, a realistic picture of Arab culture in the late pre-Islamic period must also show the living relationship between language, culture, and the history of pre-Islamic society as a whole.
We will therefore proceed along two paths, the first serving as an introduction to the second.

First, we need a historical picture of the Arabic language as it existed in the late pre-Islamic period: the language people used to express their thoughts and feelings, and to give cultural form to their lives and activities. This was also the language in which the Qur’an was expressed, at the highest level of classical Arabic style.
Second, we need some idea of how closely the life of this language was connected to the life of the people who spoke it during the same period.

The road to a complete historical picture is a long one. It is full of unresolved problems and points that are still unclear. Following that road from the beginning all the way to the period we are studying would require a separate specialist study. So here we will take a shorter route and concentrate on the points most directly connected to our subject.

What matters to us first in the history of Arabic before Islam is the stage at which it emerged from a poorly documented earlier history. Historians and linguists have disagreed over how that earlier stage should be connected with the various “Semitic” languages, or with the languages spoken to the north and south of the Arabian Peninsula.

What concerns us is the point at which Arabic acquired an independent history of its own, both as a spoken language and as a written one. By the sixth century CE, we find it in the pre-Islamic poetry known to us and in other cultural forms attributed to that period. By the seventh century, we find it in the language of the Qur’an. And from the first Islamic century onward, we find it recorded in Islamic texts.
This is the important stage we want historical and linguistic research to help illuminate. Our present study does not need to go further back than this in the history of pre-Islamic Arabia.

We can begin by defining the language we are talking about. It is the language of the northern Arabs: the language they used to communicate with one another and, through its words and structures, to express their thoughts, feelings, and ways of life. This was the foundation of the language that later became the language of the Arab-Islamic intellectual heritage, and it is the foundation of the Arabic we speak today.

Where did this language of the northern Arabs come from, both as a language of everyday communication and as a language of literature and culture? Where did its alphabet and its particular system of writing come from? And what form had it reached during the final period before the rise of Islam?
The accounts of the early Arab chroniclers cannot provide a scientific answer. First, they are full of confusion and contradiction. Second, many of them have a legendary or supernatural character.
For a sound judgment on a question like this, we need written documents or inscriptions that actually belong to the historical period under study.
Do we possess enough such evidence to reach a firm conclusion?

Archaeological and linguistic research agrees that inscriptions have been found in Syria and the surrounding region written in the Nabataean script, from which Arabic script developed. Specialists conclude from these inscriptions that the northern Arabs knew alphabetic writing by the fourth century CE.

They also have little doubt that the language of the Nabataeans was a northern Arabic dialect. One piece of evidence is that many words found in Nabataean inscriptions are purely Arabic, such as qabr, “grave.” In some inscriptions, researchers have even noted that almost the entire wording is Arabic.
Most of these Nabataean inscriptions have been found at al-Ḥijr, Petra, the Ḥawrān region, and Sinai.

Some researchers strengthen this argument further. They maintain that the Arabs of the Hijaz used Nabataean writing in trade, and that between the end of the third century and the beginning of the fourth century CE they spread this form of writing through other parts of Arabia. As evidence, they point to two well-known texts: the Umm al-Jimāl inscription and the al-ʿUlā inscription, dated to 306 or 307.

According to this view, Nabataean writing then developed rapidly in the Hijaz because both trade and religious activity were developing rapidly there. Its use in these two areas gradually gave it a distinctly Arabic character, which had become clearly visible by the beginning of the fifth century CE.

The early Arab chroniclers gave a different account. They traced the origin of Arabic writing in the Hijaz to al-Ḥīra or al-Anbār, and they recorded many stories on the subject. But although these reports are common in their works, we have no historical evidence that proves them. At the same time, we have no historical evidence that decisively disproves them either.
Ibn Qutayba tried to combine the two views by saying that the people of Mecca learned writing from both the Nabataeans and the people of al-Ḥīra.

But this does not really solve the problem. No one disputes that the people of Mecca had contact with both. The real question is different: which form of writing gave rise to the script used by the northern Arabs before Islam and to the Arabic script that later became dominant after Islam?

Because this is a historical question, it can be settled scientifically only through decisive historical evidence. In this case, that means pre-Islamic writings from al-Ḥīra, al-Anbār, or the Nabataean regions. Only evidence of this kind can establish the origin of both the script and the written language used by the northern Arabs before Islam.

Jawād ʿAlī followed this same path in his research on the subject. His investigation concludes that no pre-Islamic written text from al-Ḥīra or al-Anbār has yet been found. In fact, we do not possess a pre-Islamic written text belonging to any Arab from Iraq.

This is despite the many reports stating that writing was widespread among the Arabs of al-Ḥīra shortly before Islam, and that many people in the Hijaz knew this form of writing, learned it, and taught it to others.
By contrast, the investigation concludes that the only written material from the pre-Islamic period that has actually reached us comes originally from Syria and the surrounding region.

These writings alone, Jawād ʿAlī says, are in our possession. They allow us to say that their authors were Arabs, that their Arabic was close to the Arabic of the Qur’an, and that they wrote in a script different from the South Arabian musnad script.

Their script, he argues, was derived from the script of the Aramaeans. Their culture was also strongly influenced by Nabataean culture because they lived close to the Nabataeans and had extensive contact and interaction with them.
But even this surviving evidence consists of no more than five texts.

The earliest dates to 250 CE. It is the text mentioned earlier under the name “Umm al-Jimāl.” It was found on the tombstone of “Fihr ibn Shalī [or Salī], tutor of Jadhīma, king of Tanūkh,” together with a Greek translation.

The text is written in letters resembling early Kufic script and in a Nabataean dialect. Jawād ʿAlī thinks its writer was probably of Arab origin because of a mistake he made in applying the rules of Nabataean writing.
Jawād ʿAlī also sees historical importance in this inscription, in addition to its linguistic importance, because it points to a connection between the Arabs of Iraq and the Arabs of Syria.
The second of these five texts is the Namāra inscription. It was written on the tomb of King Imruʾ al-Qays and dates to 328 CE.
The text is written in Nabataean script and in an Aramaic dialect, but its sentence structures are Arabic. It consists of five lines, arranged as follows:
1 — “This is the grave of Imruʾ al-Qays ibn ʿAmr, king of all the Arabs, who wore the crown.
2 — He subdued the tribes of Asad and Nizār and their kings, and defeated Madhḥij down to this day, and carried
3 — victory to the walls of Najrān, the city of Shammar. He subdued Maʿadd and appointed his sons
4 — over the tribes, making them his representatives before the Persians and the Romans. No king reached the level he reached
5 — down to this day. He died in the year 223, on the seventh day of September. May his sons be granted happiness.”
Jawād ʿAlī concludes from the sound Arabic structures in the original text that its writer, or writers, were of Arab origin.
This conclusion is strengthened by expressions in the text suggesting that the writer did not have complete command of the dialect in which he was writing and did not know it especially well.
Jawād ʿAlī also argues that the Arabic of the writer does not belong to the Arabic of the Liḥyānites, the Thamūdites, or the Ṣafaites.

One piece of evidence is the repeated use of al- as the definite article. These three other forms of Arabic used h- for this purpose, while the Arabs of the south used an n at the end of the word. According to this argument, only the classical Arabic of the Qur’an used al- as the definite article.
The Namāra inscription also contains structures and expressions that, among Arabic dialects, belong only to the classical form of Arabic later used in the Qur’an.
This suggests that the writer of the inscription either spoke a dialect close to classical Arabic or was himself a speaker of that form of Arabic.

The third of the five pre-Islamic inscriptions dates to 512 CE and is known as the Zabad inscription. It was written in Nabataean script, and its writing is close to the earliest Islamic Arabic script. But it contains little more than a number of names, some of them Arabic, including “Imr al-Qays” for Imruʾ al-Qays and “Saʿdū” for Saʿd. It begins with the words: “In the name of God.”
The fourth inscription, in chronological order, is known among Orientalists as the Ḥarrān inscription. It dates to 568 CE.
This text is especially important because it is written in an Arabic very close to the Arabic of the Qur’an. Its Nabataean script is also very close to early Islamic Arabic script.
In both language and writing, then, it gives much clearer evidence of the point at which classical Arabic and its script were beginning to separate from Nabataean language and writing.

The fifth text is known as the “Second Umm al-Jimāl” inscription because it was the second inscription found at Umm al-Jimāl. It carries no date, but the Orientalists who examined it believe it was written in the sixth century CE. Its language is close to Qur’anic Arabic and is, to a large extent, free of Nabataean influence.
These five texts are the only scientific evidence we have for this stage in the history of Arabic writing.

They suggest that the first Arabic script used by the people of the Hijaz before and after Islam developed from Nabataean script, which in turn developed from the script of the Aramaeans in Syria. This development took place against the background of close historical and commercial relations between these peoples.

The texts also suggest that the language in which they were written passed through a series of gradual stages. In chronological order, we move from a purely Nabataean language in the first Umm al-Jimāl inscription, to a mixed Nabataean-Arabic language in the Namāra inscription, and then to an Arabic largely freed from Nabataean influence in the Ḥarrān and Second Umm al-Jimāl inscriptions.
At the same time, we must take account of what historians and researchers, including many Orientalists, have said about the relationship between the Arabs and the Nabataeans.

Greek and Roman historians regarded the Nabataeans as Arabs. Orientalists, too, have argued that Nabataean civilization was Arab in its basic character, and that despite its close relationship with Rome, it preserved both its tribal features and its Arabic language.

Littmann states that Nabataean is not far removed from classical Arabic and should be regarded as one of the Arabic dialects. He also notes that the personal names found in Nabataean inscriptions are usually Arabic in origin, which he takes as evidence that the Nabataeans were Arabs and that their dialect was Arabic.
Jawād ʿAlī’s detailed comparative study in his encyclopedic work gives strong grounds for accepting these conclusions.
But scientific reasoning does not allow us to treat these five inscriptions as the final word on the origin of northern Arabic and its script.
Other possibilities remain, and future research may still uncover real evidence for them. We therefore have no good reason to reject such possibilities in advance.

What is needed is more research and excavation by Arab specialists, using the scientific and technical resources now available to them on a much greater scale than they were to the Orientalists who discovered these inscriptions in the past.

The second part of our inquiry—understanding the relationship between the life of the Arabic language and the life of the people who spoke it in the late pre-Islamic period—is also surrounded by uncertainty.

Some parts of this stage in the development of Arabic still need much more light. This is especially true of the language of pre-Islamic poetry and of the artistic prose that the early Arab chroniclers preserve in many forms, including speeches, sayings, proverbs, and stories.

Modern Arab researchers, and Orientalists before them, have long disagreed over the poetic and artistic prose texts attributed to the pre-Islamic period. The dispute concerns whether these texts really belong to that period at all.

This dispute cannot be settled scientifically unless pre-Islamic writings are discovered that contain at least some of these kinds of texts. Only then could we form a clear picture of the language used by the northern Arabs shortly before and shortly after the rise of Islam for poetry, speeches, wise sayings, proverbs, and stories.
So another gap remains after the stage partly illuminated by the five inscriptions discovered so far.

What we need are written texts from the sixth or seventh century that show Arabic within its own independent historical setting: independent from Nabataean and other languages, both in its alphabet and in the language it expressed.

It is difficult to believe that the Arabic found in the Umm al-Jimāl, Namāra, Zabad, Ḥarrān, and Second Umm al-Jimāl inscriptions was exactly the form of Arabic used by the people of Mecca in the late sixth and early seventh centuries in their correspondence, poetry, speeches, proverbs, and stories of war, mythology, and religion.

It is equally difficult to believe that the means used to record those five inscriptions—especially the Ḥarrān inscription, with its Arabic language—were not also available during the same historical period for writing other Arabic texts that had fully separated from Nabataean script and from language influenced by Nabataean.
There must therefore have been pre-Islamic Arabic writings in the language of the poetry and prose that we later find recorded in Islamic sources and in the accounts of the early chroniclers.
As long as this missing link remains missing, we have only two main sources for understanding the linguistic dimension of late pre-Islamic culture.
The first is the language of the Qur’an.
The second is the body of texts attributed to the pre-Islamic Arabs and written down by Muslims from the middle of the first Islamic century onward.

We say that these texts were written “in their language” without hesitation. Whether or not every text really dates back to the pre-Islamic period, it is not reasonable to suppose that it was composed in a language completely unknown to the people of that period, or in a language that had not already passed through many stages of development.
In other words, classical Arabic cannot simply have been born with Islam or with the later age in which texts began to be systematically written down.

For any language to reach the level classical Arabic reached in the Qur’an and in the texts transmitted and recorded after Islam, it must already have lived for a very long time among the people who used it. It must have served hundreds of generations as a means of communication and as a way of expressing every part of life: their affairs, their relationships with one another, and their relationship with the universe and with nature.
The classical Arabic that appears in the Qur’an and in these other texts was therefore the product of hundreds of generations of Arabs before Islam.
And we can in fact read traces of all those generations in the language itself.

We find ancient words belonging to some of the oldest dialects of the Arabian Peninsula. We find other words belonging to later dialects developed by new generations of Arabs in the north of the peninsula and in the neighboring regions of Iraq and Syria.

We can also see a historical distance between the older meanings of these words and the newer meanings they acquired in the language of the Qur’an and in the poetry and literary prose attributed to the pre-Islamic period immediately before Islam.
We would be able to show the extent of this development, and some of its stages, much more clearly if we possessed writings from the time when Islam appeared and from the lifetime of the Prophet.
Here too, then, we face a missing link. We need written documents that belong to this precise historical setting.
